title: Beginner Grow Guides
subtitle: Start simple. Measure first. Change with a reason.
intro: These pathways help a new grower move from setup to observation without memorizing recipes. Each pathway gives four concrete steps, two common mistakes to avoid, one readiness task, and a direct link to the deeper THC learning system.
rules: Know the plant stage before changing the plan.
Write down what changed before trying to fix what changed.
Use measurements with units, location and time whenever possible.
Avoid changing several variables at once when one controlled change can answer the question.
Treat cultivar, media, water and environment as context; copied targets are starting hypotheses, not universal rules.

pathways.title: Build a Safe, Measurable Grow Space
pathways.goal: Make the space safe to operate and easy to measure before plants depend on it.

steps.title: Map power, water and access
steps.action: List major electrical loads, water sources, drains, walkways, shutoffs and anything that could become a heat or leak hazard.
steps.check: You can reach service points without moving plants or crossing wet areas with electrical equipment.

steps.title: Place sensors by purpose
steps.action: Choose canopy-level locations for temperature/RH and identify where light, root-zone and water measurements will be taken.
steps.check: A sensor location answers a defined question instead of simply being convenient.

steps.title: Plan airflow and moisture removal
steps.action: Separate equipment that circulates air from equipment that actually exchanges or removes heat and moisture.
steps.check: You can explain what happens when humidity rises rather than only pointing to a fan.

steps.title: Run the room empty
steps.action: Operate lights, climate equipment and normal loads together before plant entry and record conditions over time.
steps.check: The room completes a realistic run without unresolved safety or environmental holds.

mistakes: Buying plants before proving the room can operate safely.
Treating one wall-mounted room sensor as the whole canopy environment.
pathways.capstone: Create a one-page grow-space map showing equipment, sensors, water, power, access and the first measurements you will record.

pathways.title: Read Plant Stage Before Acting
pathways.goal: Use observable development to decide what information matters next.

steps.title: Identify the current stage
steps.action: Record whether the plant is germinating, establishing as a seedling/clone, vegetative, transitioning, flowering, finishing or recovering.
steps.check: The stage is based on visible development rather than age alone.

steps.title: Locate new growth
steps.action: Inspect shoot tips, nodes, branch growth and new leaves before judging older tissue.
steps.check: You know whether symptoms affect old tissue, new tissue or the entire plant.

steps.title: Compare growth over time
steps.action: Use dated photos or simple height/node/branch observations to see whether growth is accelerating, stable or declining.
steps.check: Your conclusion uses more than a single-day impression.

steps.title: Match the next measurement to stage
steps.action: Choose the next useful measurement from light, environment, water/root zone, plant health or maturity based on the current stage.
steps.check: You can explain why that measurement matters now.

mistakes: Diagnosing every yellow leaf without considering natural age or tissue position.
Using a fixed calendar as proof that every plant should be at the same developmental point.
pathways.capstone: Build a seven-day plant-stage photo and observation record that shows what changed and what stayed stable.

pathways.title: Seeds, Clones & Early Establishment
pathways.goal: Protect identity and release young plants by observed readiness instead of elapsed days.

steps.title: Label the source
steps.action: Record cultivar/source, seed lot or donor plant, date started and unique plant or batch ID.
steps.check: Every plant can be traced back to its source.

steps.title: Watch water status, not just humidity
steps.action: Observe media moisture, leaf posture and root development while keeping the propagation environment stable enough to compare days.
steps.check: You are not using dome humidity as the only indicator of plant water status.

steps.title: Look for establishment evidence
steps.action: Record emergence, new leaf growth, roots where visible and the plant response between irrigation events.
steps.check: Release criteria include active growth or rooting evidence.

steps.title: Acclimate after the plant proves ready
steps.action: Increase exposure to the next light/environment gradually while watching posture and growth.
steps.check: The plant is moved forward because it is responding well, not because a calendar date arrived.

mistakes: Losing plant identity by using temporary or duplicated labels.
Moving clones or seedlings into a much harsher environment in one step.
pathways.capstone: Complete one propagation batch card from source identity through release decision and first post-release check.

pathways.title: Understand the Light the Plant Receives
pathways.goal: Move beyond fixture wattage and learn to describe crop-plane light and duration.

steps.title: Know PPFD versus wattage
steps.action: Treat wattage as equipment input and PPFD as photons arriving at the measured crop position.
steps.check: You do not use watts as a substitute for canopy intensity.

steps.title: Measure more than one point
steps.action: Use a repeatable grid or at minimum compare center, edge and representative plant positions.
steps.check: Your light description includes spatial variation.

steps.title: Record photoperiod
steps.action: Write the actual light-on and light-off timing and verify the controller follows it.
steps.check: DLI or daily exposure calculations use the actual duration.

steps.title: Watch plant and temperature response
steps.action: Compare leaf posture and leaf/air temperature after meaningful light changes.
steps.check: A light adjustment is evaluated with plant and environmental response.

mistakes: Assuming the fixture manufacturer’s center reading represents the whole canopy.
Increasing intensity without rechecking leaf temperature or environmental demand.
pathways.capstone: Make a simple crop-plane light map and calculate or document the daily light period used for that map.

pathways.title: Temperature, Humidity, Airflow & VPD
pathways.goal: Describe the environment the plant experiences rather than chasing one target number.

steps.title: Record temperature and RH together
steps.action: Log both values with location and time, including at least one lights-on and one transition period.
steps.check: The reading can be placed in space and time.

steps.title: Inspect canopy microclimates
steps.action: Compare room air with at least one interior/edge canopy location where foliage changes mixing.
steps.check: You know whether room averages hide a wetter, hotter or cooler zone.

steps.title: Use VPD as context
steps.action: Use VPD to describe atmospheric demand while also checking leaf temperature, roots, irrigation and plant posture.
steps.check: You do not diagnose the plant from VPD alone.

steps.title: Watch transitions
steps.action: Record how quickly temperature/RH changes around lights-off, lights-on or irrigation.
steps.check: You can identify the fastest environmental shift in the day.

mistakes: Treating VPD as a diagnosis rather than an environmental descriptor.
Trying to solve excess moisture only by moving the same humid air faster.
pathways.capstone: Create a one-day climate timeline with at least three locations or time windows and write the most important difference you found.

pathways.title: Water, pH, EC & the Root Zone
pathways.goal: Track the water and root environment as connected measurements instead of reacting to one runoff number.

steps.title: Know the source water
steps.action: Record source, pH, EC and any available alkalinity/hardness information separately.
steps.check: You can explain that pH, EC, alkalinity and hardness are different properties.

steps.title: Use controlled meters
steps.action: Calibrate/store pH and EC instruments according to their requirements and record calibration date/result.
steps.check: A questionable meter result can be traced to a calibration record.

steps.title: Define the irrigation event
steps.action: Record volume applied, timing, media/container and how drainage or dryback is observed.
steps.check: Another person could repeat the same observation method.

steps.title: Look for trends
steps.action: Compare several sequential root-zone or irrigation records before deciding whether a change is persistent.
steps.check: You can identify an outlier without treating it automatically as a trend.

mistakes: Treating pH as if it measures nutrient concentration or alkalinity.
Comparing runoff, slurry, pore-water or feed readings as if sampling method does not matter.
pathways.capstone: Complete a seven-day irrigation/root-zone log with source water, applied solution, method and plant-response notes.

pathways.title: Nutrition Without Symptom Guessing
pathways.goal: Understand nutrient delivery while keeping environmental and root causes in the differential diagnosis.

steps.title: Know what is being applied
steps.action: Record products/inputs, mix sequence, water source, final EC/pH and volume rather than only writing a recipe name.
steps.check: The mix can be recreated from the record.

steps.title: Inspect symptom location and pattern
steps.action: Record whether symptoms begin on older/newer tissue, one plant/many plants, edge/center or one irrigation zone.
steps.check: The pattern is documented before a nutrient label is assigned.

steps.title: Check roots, water and environment
steps.action: Compare root-zone condition, irrigation history and environmental measurements before changing feed strength.
steps.check: At least one non-nutrient alternative has been considered.

steps.title: Verify after one justified change
steps.action: Define what improvement should look like and when it will be checked after an intervention.
steps.check: Success is based on follow-up evidence, not the act of feeding itself.

mistakes: Matching a leaf color to one deficiency chart and skipping root/environment checks.
Stacking multiple supplements so the cause of improvement or worsening cannot be separated.
pathways.capstone: Build a one-page differential table for one common leaf symptom with at least four candidate causes and the evidence needed to separate them.

pathways.title: Plant Health, Scouting & IPM
pathways.goal: Find problems earlier and preserve enough evidence to choose the right next step.

steps.title: Use a repeatable scouting route
steps.action: Inspect the same zones, representative leaves, undersides, stems, media surfaces and traps on a defined schedule.
steps.check: A finding can be mapped back to a location.

steps.title: Separate observation from ID
steps.action: Record what is seen, then mark organism/cause as confirmed, suspected or unknown.
steps.check: Confidence is visible in the record.

steps.title: Protect clean areas
steps.action: Use clean-to-suspect movement, tool hygiene and quarantine when spread is plausible.
steps.check: The investigation does not create avoidable cross-contamination.

steps.title: Verify control results
steps.action: Define the next scouting date and what count/pattern change will show improvement or failure.
steps.check: A treatment does not disappear from the record after it is applied.

mistakes: Spraying first and identifying later, destroying useful evidence.
Assuming one sticky trap represents pest pressure everywhere in the crop.
pathways.capstone: Complete a ten-location scouting sheet with mapped findings, confidence level, photos/samples and follow-up date.

pathways.title: Training, Canopy Shape & Recovery
pathways.goal: Use training to solve a measured architecture problem while protecting plant recovery and canopy access.

steps.title: Define the goal first
steps.action: Write whether the objective is height, spacing, support, access, branch position or light distribution.
steps.check: You can measure whether the objective was achieved.

steps.title: Document the plant before stress
steps.action: Record active tips, nodes, branch angles, plant vigor and any existing symptoms before cutting or bending.
steps.check: There is a before record for comparison.

steps.title: Make the smallest useful intervention
steps.action: Choose positioning, support, pruning or topping based on the stated goal rather than technique popularity.
steps.check: The intervention removes or damages no more tissue than needed for the objective.

steps.title: Wait for recovery evidence
steps.action: Track posture, new extension, wounds and irrigation response before adding another high-stress intervention.
steps.check: Recovery is demonstrated by the plant rather than a fixed waiting period.

mistakes: Choosing a training technique before defining the architecture problem.
Stacking topping, heavy pruning and environmental changes before the plant recovers.
pathways.capstone: Document one training intervention with goal, before photo/map, method, recovery checks and after photo/map.

pathways.title: Finish, Harvest & Plan the Next Cycle
pathways.goal: Use representative maturity observations, clean handling and final records to finish one cycle and improve the next.

steps.title: Sample maturity representatively
steps.action: Inspect more than one flower position and track observations over time rather than choosing one convenient top.
steps.check: The maturity record includes location, date and magnification/context.

steps.title: Use multiple indicators
steps.action: Combine flower development, trichome/stigma observations, cultivar context and trend without assigning universal effect claims to one color percentage.
steps.check: No single visual cue is treated as complete proof.

steps.title: Preserve lot identity through drying
steps.action: Record harvest identity, sanitation, drying environment and observations until storage/release.
steps.check: Finished material can be traced back to its plant or lot record.

steps.title: Review the cycle before repeating it
steps.action: List what worked, what failed, measurements you lacked and one change to test next cycle; for outdoor plans add site, season, weather, pollen and water context.
steps.check: The next-cycle plan is based on recorded evidence instead of memory alone.

mistakes: Using a fixed week or universal amber percentage as the only harvest decision.
Starting the next crop without reviewing records from the previous one.
pathways.capstone: Write a one-page end-of-cycle review with harvest evidence, drying/handling notes, biggest uncertainty and the single most useful improvement for the next cycle.
